DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26

## Overall assessment

Reminders are cheap, and extending them may well be worthwhile. But the report draws a causal conclusion that its own data do not support. It also contains an arithmetic error that reverses one of its headline claims. The recommendation could survive in a modified form, but its reasoning and expected benefits need substantial revision before going to the Health and Wellbeing Board.

## 1. Arithmetic error: overall uptake is 62.4%, not 66.0%

From Table 1, all schools: 13,772 vaccinated ÷ 22,080 eligible = **62.4%**. The group rows sum correctly (9,120 + 12,960 = 22,080; 6,384 + 7,388 = 13,772), so the error is in the "All schools" uptake figure.

The consequences:
- Eastvale is **below** the national 65% ambition, not above it. The Section 3 claim and the author's "building on success" framing should be removed.
- The figure of 66% doesn't follow from any obvious calculation. Even the unweighted mean of the two groups is only 63.5%, so the source of the figure should be traced.

A smaller point: non-reminder consent return is 7,970 / 12,960 = 61.5%, which would normally round to 62%, not 61%.

## 2. The 13-point gap is not evidence of a 13-point effect

This is the central problem. Schools **chose** to opt in, and Section 2 shows they differ systematically from the others:

- **School nurses:** 29 of 38 reminder schools (76%) had a full-time school nurse, compared with 11 of 54 (20%) non-reminder schools.
- **Affluence:** reminder schools are concentrated in the more affluent west. Section 4 shows that non-reminder schools serve more families who don't speak English at home and more mobile households.
- **Phone coverage:** 93% of reminder-school families have a valid mobile number on record, compared with 61% in non-reminder schools.

Each of these factors plausibly raises consent return on its own. The 13-point gap is the combined difference between two different populations of schools, and the reminder effect could be anywhere from near zero to 13 points. Statements like "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points" and "the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake" are not justified. The author's description of this as a "clean side-by-side comparison" is also inaccurate: it is observational and confounded.

Missing analyses that would help:
- **Prior-year uptake for the same schools.** If reminder schools were already about 10 points ahead in 2024-25, the reminder effect is small. A before/after comparison across both groups (difference-in-differences) is the minimum needed.
- **Adjustment for confounders.** Compare reminder and non-reminder schools within strata of nurse presence and deprivation, or use a simple regression.
- **Per-school results.** Non-reminder schools range from 38% to 79%, so some non-reminder schools out-perform the reminder average. That spread suggests school characteristics matter a great deal.

## 3. The projection to 70% ignores the report's own Section 4

The recommendation assumes non-reminder schools will rise from 57% to about 70%. Section 4 explains why that is unlikely:

- **Reach:** a text can't reach the 39% of families without a valid mobile number. Even if reminders worked equally well for everyone reached, the maximum effect is diluted by at least a third.
- **Language:** the report doesn't say whether messages or the portal are translated. English-only texts may have little effect in the wards with the most non-English-speaking households.
- **Incomplete forms:** paper forms returned with blank medical histories won't be fixed by a reminder to return consent. This is a form-completion problem, not a return problem.
- **Mobility:** with high household turnover, contact details go stale quickly.

So the populations with the lowest uptake are the least reachable by this intervention. "Bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" is not a supportable expectation. Reminders could even widen the east-west gap if they mainly help families who were already easier to reach.

## 4. "Consent is the binding constraint" is overstated

The 92%+ consent-to-vaccination rate is correct (93.3% and 92.7%). But:

- It is unclear whether "Consents returned" includes forms **declining** vaccination. If it does, the true bottleneck may be refusal rather than non-return, and reminders don't address refusal.
- Section 4 says mop-up sessions add 3–6 points but ran in only 14 schools. That is an attendance and capacity lever the report sets aside.
- The claim that reminders beat "any other intervention we have tried" is unsupported. No other interventions are evaluated, and the mop-up estimate isn't compared on the same basis.

## 5. Cost section: figures check out, framing does not

- Non-reminder schools: 12,960 − 7,970 = 4,990 non-consenting children × 3 × £0.08 = £1,198. ✔
- Existing schools: 2,280 × 3 × £0.08 = £547. ✔
- Total first year: £1,198 + £547 + £2,500 = about £4,250, which is under £5,000. ✔

However:
- The estimate counts children, not families. Siblings mean fewer messages are actually needed. Missing mobile numbers mean even fewer can be sent, which means fewer messages and also less effect.
- "Cautious" is the wrong word. The estimate overstates message volume but ignores other costs: staff time, data cleansing to raise the 61% mobile coverage, translation, and portal support.
- The useful metric is **cost per additional child vaccinated**, which depends on the true effect. That effect is what the report hasn't established.

## 6. Recommendations for revision

1. Correct overall uptake to 62.4% and remove the claim about the national ambition.
2. Recast the 13-point gap as an unadjusted association, and state the confounders explicitly.
3. Add prior-year comparisons and adjusted or stratified analyses before quoting any effect size.
4. Consider a **staged or randomised rollout** across the 54 schools in 2026-27, such as a stepped-wedge design. This would cost little and would finally produce a genuinely clean estimate.
5. Pair reminders with measures aimed at the eastern wards:
   - improving mobile-number coverage
   - translated messages and portal
   - help completing paper forms
   - more mop-up sessions
6. Set a realistic, evidence-based target rather than assuming 70%.

**Bottom line:** extending reminders is low-risk and reasonable. But the case as written overstates both the current position (62.4%, not 66%) and the likely benefit, and it under-weights its own evidence about who is not being reached.
